title: What remembering does
hookLine: in remembering God there is no pain, and death does not frighten (Sukhmani 1)

lines: AN UMBRELLA DOESN'T STOP THE RAIN.
IT CHANGES WHAT THE RAIN DOES TO YOU.
cards: An umbrella doesn't stop the rain. It doesn't shorten the storm or change the forecast. It changes one thing: what the rain does to you.
You walk the same street, in the same weather, and arrive less soaked. Much of what people carry through a hard day works like that: a hand to hold, a song, a photo in a wallet.
The first ashtpadi of Sukhmani lists, line after line, what remembering God does for the one who remembers. Read closely, it sounds less like a forecast and more like an umbrella.

teach.h: PRABH KAI SIMRAN: IN GOD'S REMEMBRANCE.
teach.b: The phrase is prabh kai simran: in the remembrance of God.

teach.h: LINE AFTER LINE ON ONE BEAT.
teach.b: The second stanza of the first ashtpadi hangs line after line on it. In paraphrase: in the remembrance of God, one does not enter the womb again. In the remembrance of God, the pain of death flees, and death is set aside.
Enemies turn back; no obstacle blocks the way. One stays awake day and night.

teach.h: FEAR DOES NOT TOUCH; SORROW DOESN'T BURN.
teach.b: In the remembrance of God, fear does not touch you, and sorrow does not burn.
The stanzas that follow keep the drum going through the rest of the ashtpadi: in God's remembrance come wisdom, meditation and understanding; the remembering one becomes truly wealthy, truly honored.
Notice what the list is doing. It isn't promising that nothing bad will happen.

teach.h: NOT NO PAIN: PAIN IN ITS PLACE.
teach.b: Sikhs who read Sukhmani in hospital rooms know that pain and loss still come. It describes what changes inside the one who remembers.
Fear loses its grip. Death, which frightens everyone, is set aside: not abolished, but put in its place.
Sikhs believe remembering God frees the soul from the round of birth and death, which is why the stanza speaks of the womb.
And on an ordinary day, it means this: the one who remembers carries something the frightening thing can't reach.

how: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite these stanzas of the first ashtpadi with their repeated opening, prabh kai simran, and many turn to them especially in times of illness or fear.

o: a charm that stops anything bad from happening
remembrance of God, which loosens fear's grip
the funeral prayers said for the dead

games.q: in the remembrance of God — tap the pairs.

s: the stanza promises that nothing bad will ever happen
it describes what changes in the one who remembers: fear loses its grip.
line after line of the stanza begins with the same phrase
prabh kai simran: in the remembrance of God.
the stanza speaks of not entering the womb again
Sikhs believe remembering God frees the soul from the round of birth and death.

games.q: something frightening is ahead of you. what does Sukhmani's first ashtpadi say about remembering God?
o: fear does not touch the one who remembers.
you should ignore the frightening thing.
games.why: prabh kai simran: in the remembrance of God, fear does not touch, and sorrow does not burn.

practice: Bring to mind something that frightens you a little, a test result, a bill, a long night ahead, and look at it without pushing it away.
Then, on each out-breath, say Waheguru if you pray, or simply the word remembering, four or five times, the hard thing still in view, and notice whether its grip loosens even slightly.

wordCard.voice: Simran, remembrance: Sukhmani's repeated phrase, prabh kai simran, in God's remembrance fear does not touch, sorrow does not burn, and death is set aside.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhau, fear; the stanza says it does not touch the one who remembers God.

carryVoice: Your line: no fear in remembering. The storm stays; the umbrella opens. Day four hundred forty, done.

sources.ref: Gauri Sukhmani M5, ashtpadi 1, pauris 2–3, Ang 262–263
